title: Why is the RBI rethinking India's $250,000 remittance window, and where do the dollars actually go?
standfirst: Reports of a possible Rs 50 lakh sub-limit have revived the argument over India’s remittance rules. RBI’s purpose-level data show where the money goes, how investment is changing the headline, and which payments a tighter rule might affect.

short.headline: A small travel category and a growing investment channel
short.dek: The purpose split, matched changes and remitter cash-flow rules explain different parts of the same window.
short.body: LRS outflows totalled $28.98 billion in FY2025-26. Business travel and pilgrimage were 2.1% of March-August 2026 travel spending. Across matched April-August windows, capital transfers increased by $1.03 billion while the remaining purposes combined fell by about $491 million. These totals do not identify how much a per-person cap would prevent.

macha.heading: Okay bro, what does this mean?
macha.body: Paying a university and buying a foreign stock use the same LRS window. They are different decisions, and the category totals matter more than the argument about whether every dollar going out is bad. Education and other travel account for most newly classified travel spending. The sharp recent increase is in investment.
macha.soWhat: A tax credit can still tie up your cash. A travel cap can still disrupt a legitimate payment. Before judging the proposed rules, we need their actual text and information about the people the limit would affect. These tables give us the totals, not that distribution.

caveats: The reported Rs 50 lakh sub-limit is a press-reported proposal; no implementing RBI notification is established by this audit.
The travel breakdown is observable only from March 2026. Earlier education-travel and combined totals are missing, not zero.
Other travel is the source category label; the source does not separately identify holidays, cards or instruments.

The macro comparison uses gross flows for the same financial year, with different coverage and possible overlap. Private transfers are broader than household remittances. The bars cannot be added or treated as offsets.
Before-and-after TCS averages do not establish the tax's causal effect or identify remitters' tax-credit use.
The annual FY2008-09 total in Report 752 conflicts with the monthly sum. The article uses the monthly record consistently; the independent audit records the difference.
The implied INR/USD rate divides INR and USD reserve valuations and is not a customer exchange quote.
The frozen source files reconcile arithmetically; independent release verification is a separate publication requirement.
Seasonal profiles average monthly shares within each of four complete financial years. Each channel has its own annual denominator; the latest partial year is excluded.
